subject: English_grammar

I’d like you to know the story of Helen
Keller, who could neither see nor hear
from the time she was a baby. Yet the
brilliant girl was able to overcome all
those difficulties, to graduate from a
college with honours and become a
useful citizen.

subject: English_grammar
text:
| must say there was nothing wrong
with Helen Keller when she was born.
Her father and mother were very proud
of their pretty baby, who tried to say
“pa-pa” and “ma-ma”.

subject: English_grammar
text:
For nineteen months Helen grew bigger and stronger. She was able to walk
when she was a year old; she could say a few words. But one day the child fell
ill. She must have been very ill. For days she had been suffering from high fever
and soon the parents learned that their darling would never be able to see
and hear. When Helen was 6 years old, her parents took her to famous doctors
to find out if they could do something to make her hear and see again, but the
doctors could do nothing. The child was hopelessly deaf. Dr. Bell said that
Kellers should write to the Perkins Institution for the blind in Boston and ask if
they would send someone to help the child.

Discuss in pairs when and where you may use must/should/have to. Then
read the section below to check your understanding.

subject: English_grammar
text:
Must is the most commonly used modal to express certainty. It can also be
used to express necessity or strong recommendation, although people often
use the form ‘have to’.
One may use must not to prohibit actions, but this sounds very strong or rude.
It is better to use softer modal verbs such as should not or ought not to
discourage something rather than to prohibit.

subject: English_grammar
text:
64 English Grammar and Composition
Examples:
e This must be the right address! (certainty)
e Students must pass an admission to study at this school. (necessity)
e You must take some medicine for that cough. (strong
recommendation)
e Jenny, you must not play in the street! (prohibition)

subject: English_grammar
text:
Must not vs. Do not have to
Must not suggests that you are prohibited from doing something. Do not
have to suggest that someone is not required to do something.
Examples:
e You must not eat that. (It is forbidden, it is not allowed.)
e You don't have to eat that. (You can if you want to, but it is not
necessary)

subject: English_grammar
text:
Should is most commonly used to make recommendations or give advice.
It can also be used to express obligation as well as expectation.
Examples:
e When you go to Agra, you should see the Taj. (recommendation)
e You should focus more on study and less on games. (advice)
e |really should be in the class by 9.00 am. (obligation)
e By now, they should already be in Dhaka. (expectation)

subject: English_grammar
text:
Have to is used to express certainty, necessity, and obligation.
Examples:
e This answer has to be correct. (certainty)
e The milk has to be stirred continuously to prevent burning. (necessity)
e They have to leave early. (obligation)
English Grammar and Composition 65

subject: English_grammar
text:
Ought to is used to advise or make recommendations. Ought to also expresses
assumption or expectation as well as strong probability, often with the idea
that something is desirable. Ought not (without ‘to’) is used to advise against
doing something.
Examples:
e You ought to stop smoking. (recommendation)
e Robi ought to get the promotion. (It is expected because he deserves
it.)

subject: English_grammar
text:
e This piece of land ought to increase in value. (probability)
e You ought not waste your time. (advice against doing something)

Now, read the following sections to know about the use of will/would.
In certain contexts, will and would are interchangeable, but there are
differences. Notice that the contracted form 'I/ is very frequently used for will.

subject: English_grammar
text:
Will can be used to express willingness:
e I'll wash the dishes if you dry them up.
e We're going to the movies. Will you join us?
It can also express intention (especially in the first person):
I'll do my exercises later on.
It can also express prediction:
e specific: The meeting will be over soon.
e timeless: Too much rain will destroy crops.
e habitual: He will eat bananas in the morning.

subject: English_grammar
text:
Would can also be used to express willingness:
e Would you please take off your coat?
